clue.text: E.g. Red Cross wanting information for marketing firm

parts.note: the Red Cross is one example of an aid agency — hence the 'e.g.'
i = information, as on tourist signs — the letter AID AGENCY goes 'wanting'

explanation.walkthrough: The 'e.g.' is working, not decorating: the Red Cross stands for AID AGENCY, which then loses its I. Losing a letter turns one business into a very different one.
explanation.definitionFit: An ad agency is a firm that creates and places advertising — the commercial arm of marketing — so 'marketing firm' describes the business plainly.

clue.text: How Nato spells out start of attack regularly falls flat

definitions.text: How Nato spells out start of attack

parts.note: the even letters of fAlLs FlAt, taken 'regularly'

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole opening clause: on the radio, NATO says 'Alfa' for the letter A. The wordplay then finds the same word sitting in 'falls flat'.
explanation.definitionFit: ALFA is the NATO phonetic alphabet's codeword for the letter A — the 'start of attack' — so the clue asks how NATO would spell that initial aloud.

clue.text: Unfortunately it's essential to medical assessment

parts.note: hidden across the join: medicAL ASsessment

explanation.walkthrough: 'Essential to' points at the core of the words — the answer runs straight across the gap between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Alas is the sighing interjection for 'unfortunately' — each can open a sentence to lament what follows.

clue.text: Student lacks head for income-generating activity

parts.note: a learner — the L-plate sense — about to lose its top letter

explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry the 'head' is the top letter, so LEARNER loses its L. 'A nice little earner' is the idiom the definition leans on.
explanation.definitionFit: An earner — as in 'a nice little earner' — is British slang for an activity that brings money in, matching the clue's noun phrase.

clue.text: Excitedly tout candidate showing focus on achievement

parts.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

explanation.walkthrough: The electioneering surface — someone excitedly touting a candidate — supplies every letter, and 'excitedly' is the word that shakes them up.
explanation.definitionFit: A can-do attitude is an optimistic readiness to get things done, so it is a mindset focused on achieving — noun phrase for noun phrase.

clue.text: Has a go at finding these birds

definitions.meaning: to snipe at someone is to have a go at them — potshots from cover

explanation.walkthrough: Split before 'finding': a verb about criticism on one side, a wading bird on the other.
explanation.definitionFit: To snipe at someone is to have a go at them, and snipes are long-billed wading birds — a verb and a plural noun sharing one spelling.

clue.text: Capital hotel invested in fresh food store

parts.note: fresh = new
a delicatessen — it takes the H in
Hotel is the NATO codeword for H

explanation.walkthrough: Hotel for H comes from the NATO alphabet, and there is a second codeword in this corner of the grid — a setter who uses one often uses another. 'Invested in' dresses the container up as finance.
explanation.definitionFit: New Delhi is the capital of India, so the single word 'capital' defines it by example.

clue.text: Kind of crossing that's slow and boring

definitions.meaning: a crossing meant for people on foot, rather than vehicles
writing that's plodding, dull and unimaginative is often given this same label

explanation.walkthrough: Split at 'that’s': the road-safety sense on one side, the sniffy adjective on the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedestrian crossing is the road crossing made for walkers, while pedestrian as an adjective means plodding and uninspired — 'slow and boring'.

clue.text: Healthy and fit? It may be one's best feature

parts.note: healthy = strong, in rude health
a verb: clothes that suit you fit you
surface glue joining the two pieces

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fit' is the trap — paired with 'healthy' it looks like the same idea twice, but it is the tailoring verb SUIT. The question mark flags the playful definition.
explanation.definitionFit: From cards, where your strong suit holds your best cards: figuratively it is the thing you do best — your best feature.

clue.text: Silly farce about elderly relative getting bouquet

parts.note: 'silly' shuffles it, and it opens around GRAN
grandmother, tucked inside the shaken FARCE

explanation.walkthrough: The jumbled FARCE opens up to admit GRAN — 'about' says the farce goes around her. 'Bouquet' is the wine-taster's word for a scent.
explanation.definitionFit: A fragrance is a pleasant smell, and bouquet is exactly that — the scent of a wine or a bunch of flowers — noun for noun.

clue.text: Misplaced utterances end long difficult trial

parts.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Misplaced' opens the clue looking like a comment on the utterances; it is the instruction to rearrange them.
explanation.definitionFit: An endurance test is a prolonged trial of stamina — 'long' and 'difficult' each earn their place in the definition.

clue.text: More extensive work involved designing employment rules initially

parts.note: the first letters of the five words

explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' governs the whole run of five words, and the office-jargon surface keeps them looking innocent.
explanation.definitionFit: Wider means more extensive — a wider search covers more ground — comparative matching comparative.

clue.text: Summer is what new TV shows look forward to!

definitions.meaning: of the year's four seasons, spring is first and summer second

definitions.text: what new TV shows look forward to
definitions.meaning: a new show's biggest hope is getting renewed for another run after its debut year

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark admits the whimsy: neither half is a dictionary definition, but both point squarely at the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Summer is literally the year's second season, after spring; and a freshly launched TV show hopes for renewal — its second season.

clue.text: Men-only race showing lack of progress

parts.note: a stag do is a men-only party
a race = a nation, a people

explanation.walkthrough: The surface conjures a strange sporting event, but 'race' is the peoples sense, and the men-only affair is a stag night.
explanation.definitionFit: Stagnation is the state of standing still — water that no longer flows — so as a state of affairs it is a lack of progress.

clue.text: Stable worker, one unlikely to get flustered

parts.note: stable = steady, firm
a hand = a worker, as in farmhand

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that a 'stable worker' could literally be a stable hand — the same two crossword staples read as one job.
explanation.definitionFit: A steady hand is the person who stays calm when things wobble — the idiom names exactly the unflappable character the definition describes.

clue.text: Complains about empty threats by workers group

parts.note: 'empty' strips out the middle, leaving the outer T and S
TU = trade union

explanation.walkthrough: 'By' just sets the pieces side by side, with the union first even though the clue names it last. Tutting is that little click of the tongue in disapproval.
explanation.definitionFit: To tut is to make the clicking sound of disapproval — someone who tuts at a thing complains about it — third person matching 'complains'.

clue.text: Establishes repository for daily sources of astronomical data

parts.note: establishes = starts (a business, say) — it opens around CHAR
a char — charwoman — is 'a daily', the old word for a cleaner who comes each day

explanation.walkthrough: 'Daily' for a charwoman is vintage British usage and a favourite way to smuggle in CHAR. 'Repository for' is the container signal, dressed up as library language.
explanation.definitionFit: Star charts are maps of the night sky — the astronomer's working documents — so they are sources of astronomical data, plural for plural.

clue.text: A doctor's concealing soft spot for lovers

parts.note: stands as itself
DR plus the ’s — it wraps round MIRE
a mire is literally a soft spot — boggy ground

explanation.walkthrough: 'Soft spot' is the trap: it means literal soft ground, MIRE, which the doctor conceals. The affection sense of 'soft spot' belongs to the answer instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Admirers are people romantically taken with someone — secret admirers, suitors — so 'lovers' fits, plural to plural.

clue.text: Instrument on parading ground

indicators.note: anagram indicator — ground as in milled, the past tense of grind

parts.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' looks like the parade ground it sits next to, but it is the past tense of grind — the letters of 'on parading' are milled into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A grand piano is a concert-hall musical instrument, so the generic 'instrument' defines it by class — the broad word for the specific keyboard.

clue.text: Test current means of transport

parts.note: an old sense of 'to test' is to strain or burden someone heavily
I is the physics symbol for electric current

explanation.walkthrough: 'Test' is a verb here — a heavy load taxes your strength — and physics lends the I.
explanation.definitionFit: A taxi is a car for hire — a means of transport in the most literal sense, the generic phrase defining a specific vehicle.

clue.text: Pay for father to take on big city university

parts.note: pop = father — he opens up to take the letters in
NY = New York
U = university, as in degree listings

explanation.walkthrough: POP 'takes on' — swallows — New York and its U; read together the insides are NYU, the famous university. To pony up is American slang for settling what you owe.
explanation.definitionFit: To pony up is informal American English for handing over money owed — 'pony up the cash' — so it means pay, verb for verb.

clue.text: New mutiny on a reshuffle is imminent

definitions.note: ANY MINUTE NOW is an adverbial phrase while 'imminent' is an adjective, but after 'is' they fill the same slot: the announcement is imminent / any minute now.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters

explanation.walkthrough: A perfectly political surface — mutiny brewing, a reshuffle coming — with the indicator posing as a noun at the end of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Any minute now' is the idiom for something on the very point of happening, which is what 'imminent' means.

clue.text: Predator consumes only half of live ones

parts.note: the front half of LIve
the front half of ONes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Only half of' applies to each word in turn, keeping the front of both — and the predator doing the consuming in the surface is the answer itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A lion is a big-cat predator — a definition by example, since 'predator' covers many hunters and the surface even shows it feeding.

clue.text: Ran into hospital to get drug

parts.note: met = ran into, encountered
H = hospital, as on road signs

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ran into' is the past tense MET, and the road-sign H completes the street name for methamphetamine.
explanation.definitionFit: Meth is the street shortening of methamphetamine, so the generic 'drug' defines it as class to instance.

clue.text: Icon that is featured on outside of journal

parts.note: i.e. = that is — its two letters split to the two ends
a mag — magazine — is a journal

explanation.walkthrough: 'That is' for i.e. is worth banking. So is the trick underneath it: a two-letter piece can split to opposite ends of the answer, which solvers miss because they expect pieces to stay whole.
explanation.definitionFit: An icon — on a screen or in a church — is a small picture, and an image is a picture: noun for noun, the visual sense of both.

clue.text: Reverse part of extremity revealed consistently

parts.note: read backwards inside: extrEMITY REVEaled

explanation.walkthrough: A hidden answer running right to left across the join of two words — 'reverse' gives the direction, 'part of' says it is buried.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Every time' means on each occasion without fail — he wins every time / he wins consistently — an adverbial phrase matching the adverb.

clue.text: Philosophy advocating a stripped-down life?

parts.note: literally a life with the clothes stripped off
the -ISM ending: a doctrine with advocates

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stripped-down' usually means pared back to essentials; here it is literal — a life with no clothes on. The question mark signals the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: Nudism is the practice — its followers would say philosophy — of living unclothed, so 'a stripped-down life' describes it both literally and punningly.

clue.text: If necessary move slowly after a knock

parts.note: stands as itself
a tap is a light knock
to inch along is to move slowly

explanation.walkthrough: 'After' inverts the order you read the clue in, which is the whole difficulty here. Note too that the definition is the entire phrase 'If necessary', not the single word 'If'.
explanation.definitionFit: 'At a pinch' is the British idiom for 'if absolutely necessary' — both slot into a sentence the same way: it will do at a pinch.
